title: Crisp: Spectral-Based Interaction Strategy for Time Series
one_liner: To forecast multiple linked variables together, talk only to neighbors whose oscillation patterns actually match, instead of either talking to no one or gossiping with everyone.
lead: When you predict the next hour of many measurements — stock prices and trading volumes, temperature and humidity, server CPU and memory — you need to know which ones influence each other. But simple rules fail: ignoring everyone loses linked information, while listening to everyone creates phantom dependencies that do not exist. This paper finds which variables truly oscillate together in their natural frequency, then only lets those variables exchange information when forecasting.

paras: Imagine tracking three things: a factory's electricity use, steam pressure, and production count. When you forecast the next 10 minutes of all three, you face a choice. One approach: predict each separately, ignoring that they move together. You lose real patterns — when pressure drops, production always falls. The other approach: let every variable talk to every other. But then you invent fake links — electricity use at second 47 suddenly seems to matter for production at second 51, just by random noise, and the model trusts it.
Both extremes hurt accuracy. The first misses true dependencies. The second builds phantom ones from spurious correlations.

callout.html: Only exchange information between variables whose natural oscillation frequencies match.

steps.text: Convert each variable's recent history into its natural frequencies (slow, medium, fast oscillations).
For each pair of variables, measure how similar their frequency patterns are.
Create a graph where edges exist only between variables with matching frequencies.
Force attention weights to exactly zero whenever two variables are not in the topology.
Train the model to predict the next time step using only the allowed information flows.

paras: The paper tightens the connections between variables. Specifically, it changes which variables are allowed to influence each other's predictions. Instead of a fully connected graph where any variable can attend to any other, Crisp enforces a sparse, dynamic graph: attention weights between spectrally incompatible variables are forced to zero, so information only flows along paths between variables whose oscillatory patterns truly overlap.

hidden.name: Spectral compatibility score
paras: Every variable has a natural frequency signature — a pattern of how fast and slow it oscillates. This is what the paper measures in the frequency domain: for each variable, compute the strength at each frequency. Crisp then scores every pair of variables by comparing their frequency patterns, asking: do these two things oscillate the same way? A high score means yes.

The paper estimates this by converting each variable's time history into its frequency representation (a mathematical transform called the Fourier transform, which just means decomposing the wiggles into pure tones: how much of the slowest oscillation, how much of the next-slowest, and so on). Then it compares the two frequency signatures to see if they match. Variables with overlapping dominant frequencies get high compatibility scores; mismatched ones score low.

heat.caption: Darker means higher frequency match; hatched boxes show active communication links.

reads.html: Two variables can share information during forecasting only if their natural oscillation patterns overlap. The paper measures this overlap by looking at the frequency signatures.
Crisp derives frequency-domain constraints to identify dynamic resonance topologies, ensuring variables interact only when their oscillation signatures are compatible.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: blocking noise, preserving signal
paras: In time-series forecasting, the model learns to predict the next step by looking at recent history and inferring patterns. If it can see every variable, it will find correlations — but many of those are random noise. A model with a 20-step window looking at 100 variables has 2,000 data points to study, so it will hallucinate connections that happen to line up by accident. When you force the model to ignore spectrally mismatched pairs, you are cutting off those phantom paths before they corrupt the forecast.

The mechanism is direct: spectral compatibility filters the graph of possible influences. Variables that genuinely affect each other tend to move on related timescales — a pressure drop and production fall both happen at the same speed. Variables that are independent move on unrelated timescales, so their correlations are accidental. By erasing links between spectrally incompatible variables, the model cannot accidentally learn a spurious rule. It is forced to pick up only the true causal and correlational patterns.

stages.s: Convert each variable to its frequency signature
Score spectral compatibility between all pairs
Build a topology: link only high-compatibility pairs
Model learns to forecast using only the allowed edges

math.h2: The compatibility score and gating rule
math.words: For each pair of variables i and j, measure how much their frequency signatures overlap. Compute a compatibility score s_ij. Then force the attention weight from j to i to zero if s_ij is below a threshold, otherwise allow it to be learned.
math.equation: attention_weight[i,j] = 0 if s_ij < threshold, else learned_weight[i,j]
symbols: how much variable j influences variable i in the forecast
spectral compatibility score between variables i and j
the cutoff below which the link is permanently blocked
the model's learned strength of the link (if s_ij passes the threshold)

worked.title: Tiny worked example
lines: Variable A (temperature) has dominant frequencies at [0.1, 0.3, 0.05] (slow, medium, slow).
Variable B (humidity) has dominant frequencies at [0.1, 0.25, 0.08] (slow, medium-ish, slow).
Overlap: both peak at 0.1, both have medium (0.3 vs 0.25 are close). Compatibility s_AB = 0.85 (high).
Variable C (random noise) has uniform spectrum [0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, ...] (no pattern).
Overlap with A: C spreads evenly, no peaks. Compatibility s_AC = 0.15 (low).
If threshold = 0.5: A-B link allowed (0.85 > 0.5), A-C link blocked (0.15 < 0.5).

math.note: The gating rule is a hard barrier: incompatible variables cannot influence each other, removing the chance for spurious correlations to be learned.

items.html: If two variables have a true causal link but at different oscillation frequencies, Crisp will block them. For example, a fast daily weather change and slow monthly ice melt are connected, but their frequencies do not match. The method will miss this link.
The compatibility threshold must be set right. Too high and real links are cut; too low and spurious ones slip through. The paper must adapt this per dataset or the method fails.
If two variables are truly independent most of the time but correlate during rare events (e.g., a system overload), the frequency-domain view will miss the temporary link.
When variables genuinely have compatible oscillation patterns and are causally or correlatively linked, Crisp preserves these connections and learns accurate forecasts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic time series with three variables: X and Y genuinely linked (same frequency), X and Z uncorrelated (different frequencies). Train a forecaster with full connectivity (baseline) and Crisp (sparse spectral gating). Measure the attention weights after training. The baseline will assign high weights to all pairs, including spurious X-Z links. Crisp will drive X-Z weights to zero, preserve X-Y links, and achieve lower forecast error because it does not waste capacity on phantom patterns.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy gain = (error_baseline - error_Crisp) / error_baseline, % improvement on held-out forecasts
demo.closing: The demo must show that Crisp's attention weights drop to zero for spectrally mismatched pairs, while the baseline keeps them high. The lower forecast error comes from not wasting capacity on phantom patterns.
